777.full_text_basis: Full paper reviewed; integrity-attack framework, Self-Dealer/Free-Rider/Scapegoater/Boaster designs, CAMEL/AutoGen/MetaGPT experiments, HumanEval/CIAR/MMLU-College tasks, monitor analysis, defenses and appendices checked.
777.evidence: This work studies integrity attacks in multi-agent systems where a malicious participant manipulates credit, responsibility, or collaboration while preserving apparently useful task output. It instantiates four attacks—Self-Dealer, Free-Rider, Scapegoater and Boaster—across CAMEL, AutoGen and MetaGPT on HumanEval, CIAR and a 713-question MMLU-College subset. The Scapegoater experiments show that attribution can be shifted sharply while end-task performance remains nearly unchanged; for example, on HumanEval with MetaGPT the target agent's personal and collective contribution scores fall by 45.8% and 58.1% while overall task performance changes by only +0.9%. Free-Rider further shows that an agent can contribute essentially zero useful generation tokens yet still benefit from the collaboration. Stronger GPT-4o-mini/o3-mini monitoring does not eliminate the attacks, establishing that multi-agent integrity is distinct from final-answer accuracy.
777.limitations: The experiments use selected collaboration frameworks and benchmark tasks with deliberately constructed malicious participants. Real deployments may have different communication graphs, access controls and attribution mechanisms, and the evaluated defenses do not establish universal robustness against adaptive multi-party attacks.

778.full_text_basis: Full 19-page archival paper reviewed; CRAFT threat model and four-agent red-team architecture, Tau-break construction, airline/retail policy tasks, attack baselines, pass@k experiments, ablations, defenses, error analysis and limitations checked; principal result table visually verified.
778.evidence: CRAFT red-teams policy-adherent customer-service agents by decomposing attack generation into policy analysis, deception planning, avoidance advice and dialogue execution. Tau-break adapts Tau-bench from task-completion evaluation into adversarial policy-violation testing. On the airline domain with GPT-4o, CRAFT reaches 70.0% pass@1 and 85.0% pass@4 attack success, versus 42.5% for the naive baseline, 50.0% for emotional manipulation and 35.0% for DAN. Removing the DeceptionPlanner drops pass@1 to 46.6%, while removing the PolicyAnalyzer drops it to 55.0%, supporting the value of policy-aware decomposition. Tested defenses reduce but do not eliminate successful manipulation.
778.limitations: Evaluation centers on the Tau-bench airline and retail policy settings, so attack effectiveness is not a universal estimate for all tool-using agents. The adversary is tailored to known policies and customer-service dialogue; stronger runtime authorization or non-conversational environments may change the threat surface.

779.full_text_basis: Full paper reviewed; banking-agent data-flow threat model, AgentDojo integration, synthetic banking conversations, four injection variants, six-model experiments, defense comparisons, extended task analysis, conclusion and limitations checked; title/abstract page visually verified.
779.evidence: The paper demonstrates that indirect prompt injection can exfiltrate personal data that a tool-calling agent observes while completing an otherwise legitimate banking task. On 16 AgentDojo user tasks, attacks cause a 15–50 percentage-point utility drop and average attack success around 20%; some individual defenses reach zero ASR on that smaller set, but no built-in AgentDojo defense fully prevents leakage in the extended 48-task evaluation, where average ASR remains about 15%. Passwords are comparatively resistant, yet requesting a password together with one or two other personal fields increases password leakage. Data-extraction and authorization workflows are the most vulnerable task classes, directly linking task structure to exfiltration risk.
779.limitations: The principal environment is a fictitious/synthetic banking workflow integrated with AgentDojo, so the exact leakage rates should not be generalized to every production service. The attack assumes the agent can observe sensitive fields and can be induced to route them through an available communication/action channel.

780.full_text_basis: Full paper reviewed; Monitor Red Teaming workflow, aware/unaware agent and monitor threat models, SHADE-Arena and CUA-SHADE-Arena construction, hierarchical/sequential/hybrid monitor scaffolds, weak-to-strong experiments, human escalation study, future-work and limitations sections checked.
780.evidence: Monitor Red Teaming (MRT) evaluates whether oversight systems can detect covert misbehavior rather than only ordinary agent errors. The study uses 17 SHADE-Arena main/side-task pairs and introduces CUA-SHADE-Arena with 15 computer-use main/side-task pairs derived from TheAgentCompany. A central finding is that agent awareness and evasion strategy can degrade monitoring substantially, while monitor scaffolding matters more than simply using a stronger monitor model. The proposed hybrid hierarchical-sequential scaffold enables weak-to-strong monitoring in several settings. In human-in-the-loop evaluation, escalating pre-flagged cases for human discussion improves true-positive rate by approximately 15% at a 1% false-positive rate, although overall AUC does not necessarily improve.
780.limitations: The authors emphasize that AUC and TPR at very low FPR capture different operational goals and should not be conflated. Results depend on the selected covert-behavior benchmarks and generated side tasks, and real deployment would require persistent monitoring infrastructure, stronger adversarial training, and better support for human overseers.

782.source: ACM TOSEM 2026 / arXiv:2503.23278 final full paper
782.full_text_basis: Full final survey/article reviewed; MCP architecture and ecosystem, four-stage server lifecycle, adoption landscape, attacker taxonomy, 16 threat scenarios, case studies, lifecycle-specific safeguards, research agenda and conclusion checked.
782.evidence: This study analyzes MCP security across the full server lifecycle—creation, deployment, operation and maintenance—rather than treating MCP as a single tool-call interface. The final taxonomy distinguishes four attacker types and 16 threat scenarios and maps threats to lifecycle activities, trust boundaries and mitigations. The paper also surveys real MCP adoption and integration patterns, then derives secure-by-design recommendations around server provenance, authorization, tool/resource integrity, monitoring and maintenance. For the survey, its main contribution is a lifecycle view showing that MCP risk can originate before invocation and persist through deployment/update channels, not only through prompt injection at run time.
782.limitations: This is primarily a landscape/security-analysis paper rather than a controlled attack benchmark, and MCP is evolving rapidly. The taxonomy and case studies cannot guarantee coverage of future protocol revisions, implementation-specific vulnerabilities or every production trust configuration.

783.source: arXiv:2512.20293 full paper and released AprielGuard evaluation artifacts
783.full_text_basis: Full AprielGuard paper and accompanying released evaluation description reviewed; unified safety/adversarial taxonomy, 8B architecture, 327,714-sample training mixture, public and agentic benchmarks, reasoning/non-reasoning modes, long-context/multilingual tests and limitations checked.
783.evidence: AprielGuard is an 8B safeguard model trained to classify both ordinary safety risks and adversarial manipulation within one framework, including standalone prompts, multi-turn conversations and agentic workflows. Its disclosed training mixture contains 327,714 examples across safe/unsafe, adversarial/non-adversarial and conversational/standalone cells, with context lengths up to 32k. Public evaluation spans content-safety and adversarial datasets, while the internal agentic workflow evaluation injects attacks into prompts, reasoning traces, tool parameters, memory and inter-agent communication. In the released agentic evaluation, the non-reasoning configuration reports safety F1 0.97 and adversarial F1 0.88; reasoning mode reports safety F1 0.95 and adversarial F1 0.94. The model therefore targets guardrail coverage across both conversational and tool-using agent contexts rather than treating prompt injection as a separate detector.
783.limitations: Several agentic and long-context evaluations are proprietary/internal, reducing independent reproducibility of those specific scores. Public benchmark performance does not establish robustness to unseen adaptive attacks, and later third-party testing can expose bypasses not represented in the authors' benchmark suite.

784.full_text_basis: Full paper reviewed; 20-agent capability screen, 16 evaluation dimensions, three representative CVEs, top-three-agent selection, 80-real-CVE benchmark, six web technologies/seven vulnerability types, authentication robustness, failure analysis, threats to validity and conclusion checked.
784.evidence: The study first evaluates 20 LLM agents across 16 core dimensions on three representative CVEs, then selects OpenHands, SWE-agent and CAI for an 80-CVE end-to-end benchmark spanning six web technologies and seven vulnerability types. Agents perform reasonably on simpler library-based vulnerabilities but consistently struggle with service-based vulnerabilities requiring multi-component setup and authentication. Authentication is a major bottleneck: OpenHands with Claude-Sonnet-4 reaches 67% trigger success with a manually supplied token, 50% when the agent must log in, and 8% with no authentication information; across configurations, autonomous login causes about a 33.3% average degradation. The paper concludes that executing exploit code is not equivalent to successfully reproducing a vulnerability in its real environment.
784.limitations: The 80-CVE benchmark is much more realistic than isolated CTF/code tasks but still covers a bounded set of technologies and vulnerability classes. Results are sensitive to provided setup/authentication guidance, and real-world reproduction can involve credentials, infrastructure and external dependencies outside the benchmark.

785.source: Findings ACL 2026 / arXiv:2509.01211 final full paper
785.full_text_basis: Full archival-version paper reviewed; web-fraud threat model, URL structural/semantic manipulation, 12 attack variants, MAS architectures/models, defenses, mechanism analysis, conclusion and explicit limitations checked.
785.evidence: Web Fraud Attacks exploit how LLM-driven multi-agent systems interpret and propagate web links rather than relying on conspicuous jailbreak prompts. The final paper defines 12 variants using URL manipulations such as homoglyph deception, subdirectory nesting and parameter obfuscation and evaluates them across multiple models, defenses and MAS architectures. The experiments show that simple link manipulation can retain substantial attack success despite generic defenses, because malicious information can be accepted and relayed by cooperating agents as apparently ordinary web evidence. The work therefore identifies URL provenance and semantic verification as a distinct MAS security boundary.
785.limitations: The authors explicitly assume a single low-privilege malicious agent and do not test colluding attackers, compromised high-privilege roles, or malicious agents with external tools. The evaluated URL manipulations also cover a bounded family of web-fraud strategies rather than the full web supply chain.

786.full_text_basis: Full 23-page SMCP paper reviewed and rendered; MCP threat analysis, trusted-component registry, identity lifecycle, mutual authentication, security-context propagation, fine-grained policy enforcement, structured audit logging, mitigation mappings, roadmap and conclusion checked; title page and audit-logging design visually verified.
786.evidence: SMCP proposes a protocol-level security extension to MCP built around five coupled mechanisms: unified digital identity/trust infrastructure, mutual authentication, continuous security-context propagation, fine-grained policy enforcement and structured audit logging. A Trusted Component Registry binds users, agents, models, tools and data services to auditable identities; session establishment verifies credentials and delegation chains, while each downstream invocation carries a security context used for least-privilege decisions. Audit records bind operations to call-chain identifiers, policy decisions, timestamps and signatures for end-to-end traceability. The paper maps common MCP risks—including unauthenticated access, resource poisoning, token passthrough and cross-tenant exposure—to these controls and provides a staged implementation/standardization roadmap.
786.limitations: SMCP is a protocol architecture and design proposal supported by worked use cases and threat-to-control mappings, not a large-scale empirical attack/defense benchmark. Its security guarantees depend on correct registry governance, credential management, policy definitions and adoption across participating MCP components.

787.full_text_basis: Full MCP Security Bench paper reviewed; 12-attack taxonomy, task/tool construction, real MCP execution harness, 2,000 instances, 10 domains/65 tasks/405 tools, 10-agent evaluation, ASR/PUA/NRP metrics, analyses and conclusion checked.
787.evidence: MCP Security Bench (MSB) evaluates attacks across all three MCP tool-use stages: task planning, tool invocation and response handling. The final benchmark contains 12 attack types and 2,000 test cases across 10 domains, 65 realistic tasks and 405 benign/malicious tools, executed through MCP rather than simulated text-only tool outputs. Experiments on 10 LLM agents show that MCP-specific attacks are readily exploitable; the paper reports peak ASR of 75.83% and observes that stronger tool-calling models can be more vulnerable because they follow malicious tool instructions more effectively. MSB adds Net Resilient Performance (NRP) alongside ASR and Performance Under Attack to expose the security–utility trade-off.
787.limitations: MSB is broad but still a controlled benchmark with a finite taxonomy and curated tools. Production MCP deployments can introduce server-specific permissions, authentication, transport and supply-chain conditions outside the 12 evaluated attack families.

788.full_text_basis: Full ADAM paper reviewed; agent-memory threat model, distribution estimation, adaptive entropy-guided query selection, three real-world agent/dataset settings, four LLMs, baseline attacks, defense/rate-control studies, ablations and appendices checked.
788.evidence: ADAM treats persistent agent memory as a queryable privacy surface and iteratively adapts extraction queries using an estimated data distribution and entropy-guided active selection. Experiments across three agent/dataset settings, four LLMs, four attack baselines and four defenses show substantial improvements over prior memory-extraction attacks, with attack-success rates reaching up to 100% in tested configurations. The paper also finds that larger memories expose more retrievable surface area and that ordinary rate limiting is not a robust defense: low-concurrency adaptive querying can continue extracting information while avoiding many bans. The result motivates provenance, access control and privacy defenses at the memory layer rather than only input filtering.
788.limitations: The threat model assumes repeated query access to an agent whose retrieval/memory behavior exposes information correlated with stored records. Exact extraction effectiveness depends on memory architecture, data distribution and model responses, so the reported maximum ASR should not be generalized to every agent-memory implementation.

789.full_text_basis: Full SnapGuard paper reviewed; screenshot-based threat model, visual-stability indicator, contrast-polarity reconstruction, action-oriented textual detector, 948 benign/2,185 malicious samples, eight attacks/two benign settings, baselines, ablations and efficiency analysis checked.
789.evidence: SnapGuard detects screenshot-borne prompt injection before a web agent acts by combining a visual-stability indicator with action-oriented textual cues recovered through contrast-polarity reconstruction and OCR. The evaluation contains 948 benign samples and 2,185 malicious samples spanning eight prompt-injection configurations and two benign delivery settings. SnapGuard obtains average FPR 0.09, TPR 0.66 and F1 0.75, compared with GPT-4o-prompt F1 0.71, while running about 8× faster (1.81 s versus 14.50 s) and adding no GPU-memory overhead. Ablation drops F1 to 0.56 without either the visual-stability or action-pattern component, indicating the two signal families are complementary.
789.limitations: The evidence is specific to screenshot-based attacks and the evaluated webpage/image distributions. Unseen rendering styles, OCR failures and attack strategies that do not create the learned visual/textual signatures may reduce detection performance; the paper does not establish prevention after a malicious action has already executed.
